messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Non-binary
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Authority Presence: Police, Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Eli was a 75-year-old non-binary individual of Oceania descent who sought psychological help following a traumatic rape incident. Once a dedicated financial analyst with a keen eye for detail and precision, Eli now found themselves struggling to maintain any sense of meaning in their life after the event. The trauma began on an otherwise ordinary evening when Eli was walking home from work. As they walked through a dimly lit alleyway near their office building, they were suddenly confronted by an assailant who dragged them into a secluded area. The attack was swift and brutal; the sounds of shouting, grunts, and the metallic tang of sweat in the air now replayed vividly whenever Eli attempted to recall what had transpired. Since that night, Eli has struggled with intrusive memories and flashbacks that seem to come out of nowhere. When these memories surface, they are accompanied by auditory recollections of the assailant's voice, as well as a sharp taste reminiscent of the metallic sweat that clung to their skin during the attack. Despite numerous attempts to piece together what happened, Eli cannot form a coherent narrative of the event, which only adds to their distress. The triggers for these memories are specific and potent. Eli feels particularly vulnerable when they encounter authority figures such as police officers or anyone who misbehaves in public. These triggers have led to significant avoidance behaviors; Eli has been skipping meetings at work where criticism is common, fearing that any negative feedback might trigger a flashback. This has affected their performance as a financial analyst, leading to missed deadlines and strained relationships with colleagues. Eli's interpretation of the event has also taken a toll on their self-perception. They have come to believe that they cannot rely on themselves anymore, questioning whether they can navigate life without crumbling under pressure. The constant fear of going "crazy" exacerbates this belief; Eli feels that their reactions since the assault mean there is something fundamentally wrong with them. Over time, these beliefs and fears have led to a pervasive sense of meaninglessness in their daily activities. Work no longer provides any satisfaction or purpose, and even hobbies once enjoyed now feel empty. The social circle Eli once cherished has dwindled as they have isolated themselves from friends and family, fearing that interactions might trigger distressing memories. What finally compelled Eli to seek help was a particularly vivid flashback at work. They were presenting financial data in front of their team when a colleague's critical comment set off a wave of auditory and visceral memories from the assault. This experience was so overwhelming that it left Eli unable to continue with their duties, and they felt a profound sense of shame and confusion. In seeking psychological support, Eli is most hopeful for regaining some semblance of control over their life. They are also deeply afraid of facing more flashbacks or reliving the trauma, but recognize that this fear might only worsen their situation if left unaddressed. The therapeutic journey will aim to help Eli process the traumatic event and reframe their negative beliefs about themselves and the world around them.
